Rock and roll, written by Leiber and Stoller.
Listen for the hard, stop time hits that open each verse.
items.lyr: The warden throws a party in the county jail, and the prisoners' band plays so well that everybody dances. It's a comic scene full of nicknames for the inmates, with the whole cell block dancing.

n: Blue Suede Shoes, by Elvis Presley, 1956, his cover of the Carl Perkins song.
Listen for how much more he leans into the vocal, and the hip shaking stage energy.

n: Tutti Frutti, by Little Richard, 1955.
Listen for the pounding piano and his shrieks.
items.lyr: "Tutti frutti" is an ice cream flavor, and "a-wop-bop-a-loo-bop" is pure rhythm with no meaning. He sings about two girls, Sue and Daisy, who drive him wild. The original lyrics were much ruder and were cleaned up before recording.

n: Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On, by Jerry Lee Lewis, 1957.
Rockabilly piano, from the man nicknamed The Killer.
Listen for the sweeping glissandos in his right hand, the pounding left hand, and his wild stage antics.

n: Chapter one: Roots of Rock Music.
America's first popular songs came from British and other European settlers.

Thanks to the Copyright Act of 1790, which let composers and publishers earn money from published songs, the popular music industry grew rapidly through the eighteen hundreds, and then exploded in the twentieth century with the phonograph, radio, and television.
Four styles, all established by the 1890s, directly influenced rock: ragtime, Tin Pan Alley, the blues, and jazz.
Of these, only ragtime and Tin Pan Alley were composed and sold as sheet music, while the blues and jazz were improvised.
Because the first jazz recording wasn't made until 1917, and the first blues recordings even later, the earliest forms of both are lost.
Ragtime was mainly, though not only, an African American style.
It may have started on the banjo in the mid eighteen hundreds, but piano rags became more common.
It was named for the ragged, or syncopated, melody played by the pianist's right hand, while the left hand steadily alternated between a single bass note and a chord.
Its spread was helped by new sound devices such as the player piano, the phonograph, and early jukebox type players.
Its best known composer was Scott Joplin, 1868 to 1917, whose Maple Leaf Rag, from 1899, sold more than a million copies of sheet music while he was still alive to collect royalties.

Ragtime influenced rock directly through its energy and syncopated rhythms, and also through stride piano, which developed from it and became an element of many rhythm and blues piano styles used in rock.

Tin Pan Alley was the stretch of West Twenty-Eighth Street in New York, between Fifth Avenue and Broadway, where many music publishers had their offices in the late eighteen hundreds and early nineteen hundreds.
Tin pan referred to the thin, tinny sound of the cheap upright pianos the publishers used.
Vaudeville shows needed a huge amount of new music, and since so many of them started in New York before touring the country, New York publishers gained control of the industry.
Their songs were sentimental ballads or fun, escapist songs of the gay nineties, often based on popular dance rhythms, and above all simple and easy to remember.
Take Me Out to the Ball Game, written in 1908 by Jack Norworth and Albert Von Tilzer, is one that baseball fans still know.
These catchy melodies became the model for pop oriented rock songs, ballads, and dance music.
The main difference is that Tin Pan Alley was sold as sheet music for people to play themselves, while rock was sold as records.
items.s: Take Me Out to the Ball Game

items.h: New Orleans jazz, swing, and crooners
n: By the late eighteen hundreds, musical life in New Orleans had shifted from opera to band music, with bands playing parades, funerals, picnics, and dances.
Most of the musicians were African American or Creole and had some formal training, but they began improvising on the written lines.
The African American players in particular added syncopated African rhythms and influences from the blues and black gospel, and this transformed music was called hot music.

Hot bands had a front line of one trumpet or cornet, one clarinet, and one trombone, backed by a rhythm section, the instruments that keep the beat and play the chords: banjo, guitar, or piano, string bass or tuba, and drums.
Jazz spread beyond New Orleans because African American groups toured in vaudeville and minstrel shows as early as 1908, and because social dancing became hugely popular.

Its raggy rhythms were perfect for dances like the Charleston in the twenties, and it stayed dance music through the swing era, from about 1934 to the end of World War Two, when a perfect night out meant dancing to a big band.

Swing bands were much bigger than New Orleans bands, with whole sections of trumpets, trombones, and saxophones, and they played mostly from written arrangements, leaving limited room for improvised solos.
Their smoother rhythm section used string bass, piano, and drums.
Swing also changed how the bass was played.
The old tuba bass pumped back and forth between the first and third beats of each bar, while swing bassists played a walking bass, a new note on every beat, sometimes with extra notes between beats.
Walking bass was later used in rhythm and blues and rock and roll.
Swing bands often backed singers in a new style called crooning, which developed because of a new invention, the microphone: sound engineers could amplify a soft, gentle voice better than a loud one.
So crooners softened their voices into a smooth tone and slid from note to note for a warm, sentimental effect.
Bing Crosby was one of the most popular crooners of the swing era.
Perry Como was another crooner of the swing era.
Crooners like him later influenced the teen idols of the late fifties and early sixties.

items.h: Roots of the blues · Delta blues
n: The earliest roots of the blues lie in Africa, but also in music from Arabia, the Middle East, and Spain under the Moors, where Arabic scales, Turkish ceremonial rhythms, and the rhythmic freedom of Spanish singers all resemble parts of African music and the blues.
The book finds the clearest African predecessor in the griots of Sierra Leone, oral poets who sang the history of their people and leaders.
The blues isn't just a transplanted griot song, though, because the griot was central to the dominant society, while the blues was the personal expression of people denied respect.
European church hymns also influenced the blues, giving it a three chord progression and short verses of equal length.
Slavery added two more traditions.
Work songs were sung by groups during hard labor in the African call and response style, where a leader sings a phrase and the group answers with a response.
Field hollers were sung by one worker alone, slower, freer in rhythm, and highly improvised, often lamenting the work.

Both sometimes used signifying, meaning lyrics with a double meaning, so that a song that sounded respectful to the overseer could really be about discontent, a tradition that goes back to the griots and reappears in rap.
The earliest blues came from the rural South and is called country blues, sung by performers who usually accompanied themselves on battered guitars, and it wasn't recorded until the twenties.
Most blues follows a form called the twelve bar blues.
The lyrics use an A A B pattern: the first line is sung, then repeated, and a contrasting third line answers it, often rhyming.
Each line lasts four bars of four beats, so a full verse, also called a chorus or stanza, is twelve bars.
Call and response is built into the form, because the singer sings only through the start of the third bar of each line, and an instrument, or the singer's own guitar, fills the rest as a response.

The chords follow a standard pattern: four bars of the tonic, two bars of the subdominant and two of the tonic, then the dominant seventh, the subdominant, and two final bars of tonic, though early blues players often kept the dominant through the first two bars of that last line.

The beat is usually divided unevenly, long short, long short, and when the bass plays on the beat and the chord on the short note, this is called a shuffle beat, which at slow tempos gives the blues its relaxed feel, while folk and country music divide the beat evenly.
The country blues style that most influenced rock was delta blues, from the Mississippi delta, rougher and more emotional than the country blues of places like the Carolinas.
Two more sounds to listen for.

First, many delta guitarists broke off the neck of a bottle, filed it smooth, and slid it along the upper strings, keeping their other fingers free for chords or bass lines, and later, glass and steel bottlenecks were sold for this purpose.

Second, the blues uses blue notes: the third and seventh notes of the major scale, lowered or bent in pitch, which may come from the five note pentatonic scales of much world music, or from Islamic influence on African music.

A bottleneck can slide right through blue notes that fall between the guitar's frets, and without one, a guitarist can push or pull the string to raise and lower the pitch, which is called string bending.
A piano can't bend notes, so pianists lower the note a full half step, or hit two neighboring keys at once.
Delta musicians named in the book include Robert Johnson, Charley Patton, and Son House.
We'll come back to Johnson.
First, Charley Patton.
Now Son House, who, like Patton and Johnson, accompanied his singing with strummed guitar chords mixed with melodic fills.
Not every slide player used a bottleneck.
Lead Belly, whose real name was Huddie Ledbetter, 1885 to 1949, got a similar effect by sliding a knife along the strings.

Two later musicians kept the essence of delta bottleneck guitar while updating it with amplification and other instruments: Big Joe Williams, who recorded for Vocalion as early as 1929, and Muddy Waters.
First, Big Joe Williams.
Muddy Waters began recording in 1945 for Aristocrat Records, which was renamed Chess Records in 1948.
Cross Road Blues, by Robert Johnson, 1937.
Delta blues.
Johnson was a Mississippi singer and guitarist who recorded only twenty nine songs, and legend says he sold his soul at a crossroads to play so well.
Listen for his bottleneck slide guitar answering his voice, and his free rhythm, where he adds beats and sings in a different rhythm from the one he plays.
items.lyr: A Black man stands at a crossroads as the sun goes down, trying to wave down a passing car ("flag a ride"), but nobody stops for him. Sundown matters: in the 1930s South, African Americans could be in danger if they were caught outside after dark, so he is desperate to get away before night. He falls to his knees and asks God for mercy. Beyond the literal story, the song is about loneliness and having no way out.
nl: Robert Johnson, 1911 to 1938, was one of the most influential country blues singer guitarists of the thirties.
He grew up poor on a Mississippi plantation, and his lyrics are about his appetite for wine, women, and song.
He recorded only twenty nine songs, in makeshift studios in hotel rooms and office buildings, and because big record companies weren't interested, the records were barely distributed in his lifetime.
Later reissues made him a major influence on rock musicians.
Few people heard him live, and their stories gave rise to the Faustian myth that he sold his soul to play so well, dramatized in the 1986 movie Crossroads.

Johnson used the A A B lyrics and the basic blues chords, but he wasn't bound by strict rhythm: he added extra beats and bars at random, and sometimes sang in a different rhythm from the one he played on guitar.
Using more than one rhythm at the same time is called polyrhythm, a practice known in some African traditions.
The listening guide is Cross Road Blues, from 1937, four twelve bar choruses with no other musicians, in which Johnson answers his own singing on bottleneck guitar.
The tempo is about 88 beats per minute, but he speeds up and slows down at will.
The lyrics show a lonely black man in the 1930s South who can't flag a ride and must leave the crossroads before dark, a reference to the curfews imposed on African Americans at the time.
Two years after this recording, Johnson died at twenty seven, poisoned either by a woman he was involved with or by her husband.

n: Many rock groups recorded Johnson's songs, including the Rolling Stones, Cream, and Fleetwood Mac.
First, the Rolling Stones, who recorded his Love in Vain and Stop Breaking Down.
Cream recorded Cross Road Blues, but called it Crossroads.
Fleetwood Mac recorded his Hellhound on My Trail.
Most country blues singers who caught the record companies' attention were men, but women sang the blues too, in two different ways.
Some, like Memphis Minnie, accompanied themselves on guitar in the country blues tradition.
Others, called classic blues singers, didn't play an instrument at all, but sang in front of jazz bands, so they developed powerful, gutsy voices that could be heard over the band.
Memphis Minnie, whose real name was Lizzie Kid Douglas, 1897 to 1973, recorded for many labels, including Columbia, Victor, Vocalion, OKeh, and Decca.
Most classic blues singers were from the South and grew up hearing country blues.
Two of them, Ma Rainey and Bessie Smith, inspired the later rock singers Etta James, LaVern Baker, and Janis Joplin.
We'll hear the rock singers first, starting with Etta James.
LaVern Baker.
Janis Joplin.
And now their models, starting with Ma Rainey.
Lost Your Head Blues, by Bessie Smith, 1926.
Classic blues.
Smith was called the Empress of the Blues, a singer with a huge voice built to carry over a jazz band.
Listen for the cornet answering each of her lines, which is call and response, and the A A B pattern of the lyrics, where each first line is sung twice.
items.lyr: Her man has come into money, and now he's "lost his head," meaning he's become arrogant and foolish, and he's treating her badly. She tells him she was good to him when he was poor, and now she's leaving. "Once ain't for always, and two ain't for twice" is a proverb: don't expect to get away with the same thing twice. In the last verse her days feel lonely and her nights feel long.
nl: Bessie Smith, 1894 to 1937, earned the title Empress of the Blues.
She was featured in the 1929 film Saint Louis Blues, and she died from injuries in a car accident while on a theater tour.
The listening guide is Lost Your Head Blues, from 1926, recorded with Joe Smith on cornet and Fletcher Henderson on piano.

It's a twelve bar blues with a four bar introduction and five choruses, in which the cornet plays the fill at the end of each vocal line, the call and response pattern again, while the piano accompanies without solos.
The lyrics are about money corrupting love: now that her man has money, he's deserting the woman who stood by him when he was poor.

n: Other classic blues singers included Alberta Hunter, Mamie Smith, and Ida Cox.
First, Alberta Hunter.
Mamie Smith.
Ida Cox.

items.h: Jazz singer who sang some blues
n: Billie Holiday is sometimes called a blues singer, but she recorded few songs that were technically blues, and she is better known as one of the greatest female jazz singers, recording from the thirties through the fifties.
One of her best blues recordings is her own composition, Fine and Mellow, from 1939.

items.h: The beginnings of rock and roll · Tape and echo
n: Rock also grew from styles that weren't yet nationally popular.

Delta blues and rhythm and blues were mostly played and sold in African American neighborhoods, and some country styles had only regional audiences, a division of musical tastes caused partly by racism and segregation.
Several technological changes of the late forties and early fifties were also essential.
Magnetic tape recorders greatly improved sound quality and let studios create echo effects and overdubs.
Elvis Presley's Heartbreak Hotel, from 1956, is a famous example of echo.
Overdubbing means recording new parts on top of an existing recording.
Eddie Cochran's Summertime Blues, from 1958, is a famous example: he overdubbed his own playing several times, creating a sound he couldn't have made live without other musicians.
Recordings became so central to rock that many performers lip synced to their records on television.

Three developments in 1948 were especially important: transistor radios, thirty three and a third R P M long playing albums, and forty five R P M singles, though the new records didn't fully replace the old seventy eights until 1954.
Forty fives became popular because they let people buy a single song cheaply, with another on the B side, and because jukeboxes used them.
Jukeboxes in soda fountains, restaurants, and bars let everyone in the room hear a song, even without a radio.
Racial barriers began to erode when white teenagers started listening and dancing to the rhythm and blues of jump bands like Louis Jordan and his Tympany Five in the late forties.
Radio changed in the late forties too.

Before, there were only four national stations, aimed at a white middle class audience, but then small independent stations sprang up everywhere, with disc jockeys who were entertainers in their own right and weren't afraid to play rock and black rhythm and blues.
Because rhythm and blues records were usually sold only in black neighborhoods, radio was how most white teenagers first heard them.

Televisions became affordable for average families in 1951, and as white entertainers moved their programs from radio to TV, radio had room for broader programming, while TV dance shows like American Bandstand later spread rock nationwide.

By 1951, the smooth sound of African American vocal groups like the Platters and the Moonglows reached white teens through maverick disc jockeys who refused to go along with racial exclusion, the most famous being Cleveland's Alan Freed.
First, the Platters.
Then the Moonglows.
Car radios in the early fifties, and later portable transistor radios, brought this music to more teenagers.

In 1954, the Supreme Court decided in Brown versus Board of Education that public schools must be integrated, and although integration took years, the book gives rock, which grew from both African American and white music, part of the credit for relaxing racist attitudes.
To recap chapter one.
From West African traditions, the blues took polyrhythm, blue notes, and call and response.
From European traditions, it took the regular four beat bar, the A A B lyric scheme, and the twelve bar chord progression.
As recording technology spread, blues musicians moved to cities and played with jazz bands and their instruments.

Rock grew out of the many styles of the forties, became a style of its own in the early fifties, depended on recording technology more than any style before it, and helped move America toward integration and mutual respect.
End of chapter one.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
chapters.sub: Urban Blues and Rhythm and Blues

n: Before chapter two, the book introduces the decade of the fifties.
In 1950, Americans feared the communist Soviet Union and People's Republic of China, especially since the Soviets had more planes, tanks, and troops, and had already tested an atomic bomb.
Families who could afford it built bomb shelters, and schools ran drills where children hid under their desks.

Fear of communism at home led to the execution of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg in 1953 for selling secrets to the Soviets, and to Senator Joseph McCarthy's investigations, which the Senate ended after his televised questioning of the Army that same year.
The House Un-American Activities Committee investigated the entertainment industry, and its blacklist of suspected communists destroyed many Hollywood careers and discouraged controversial subjects.
This fear lasted through the whole cold war, from 1950 to 1990.
Still, the fifties were prosperous for most white middle class Americans.

The baby boom generation was born, and parents who had worked through their own teenage years gave their children more freedom and money, so for the first time teenagers' tastes decided what was popular.

Part of that youth culture was the image of the rebellious antihero, created by movies: The Wild One in 1954, with Marlon Brando as the leader of a motorcycle gang, and in 1955, Blackboard Jungle, about juvenile delinquents, and James Dean's Rebel Without a Cause.

Rockabilly singers such as Gene Vincent and Eddie Cochran wore the black leather jackets of that image and sang about breaking free of adult authority, but the book stresses that the movies created the image, not the rock artists.
First, Gene Vincent.
Gene Vincent.
Eddie Cochran.

Rebellion wasn't limited to teenagers: the writers and poets of the Beat movement called American society hypocritical and oppressive, and their ideas later shaped folk rock, psychedelic, glitter, punk, and industrial music.
Television, by contrast, showed perfect families with no problems, in shows like Ozzie and Harriet, Father Knows Best, and Leave It to Beaver.
For African Americans, the fifties were a time of recognizing their unequal status and deciding together to change it.
In parts of the South, impossible tests and fees called poll taxes kept them from voting, and on television they were cast only as servants.
In 1954, Brown versus Board of Education forced segregated schools to integrate, although more than two thousand school districts still hadn't by 1960.

In 1955, in Montgomery, Alabama, Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat to a white man, and Doctor Martin Luther King Junior led a 381 day bus boycott, after which the Supreme Court outlawed segregated seating on public transportation.
Entertainment venues were segregated too.
At New York's famous Cotton Club, Duke Ellington and other jazz greats of the thirties played to white audiences, and African Americans weren't allowed to mix with the white patrons.
items.s: It Don't Mean a Thing (If It Ain't Got That Swing)

items.h: Salt and pepper all mixed together
n: By the fifties, some clubs had separate black nights and white nights, or roped off the dance floor to keep the crowds apart.
As white teenagers came to love rhythm and blues and blues based rock, they rejected that segregation, and gradually the separate nights merged and the ropes came down.
As Chuck Berry said at the time, what's happening, salt and pepper all mixed together.
In many ways, rock was a music of integration.
Chapter two: Urban Blues and Rhythm and Blues.
The blues grew out of slavery and the rejection African Americans still faced after freedom, but it was not always sad music.
It helped people cope with hard lives, and many lyrics looked forward to better times, while others told stories, often with sexual references.
Perhaps the first type of rock music was played by rhythm and blues musicians who added more energy and a stronger backbeat, meaning accents on the second and fourth beats of each four beat bar.
Bo Diddley is one example: a rhythm and blues guitarist and singer whose music is also early rock.
During World War One, from 1914 to 1918, many northern factory workers left their jobs to fight in Europe.
At the same time, boll weevils were destroying the cotton crops of the Mississippi delta, so many southern African Americans moved north, to cities like Kansas City, Chicago, and New York, for work.
They found less discrimination than in the South, and word spread, but neighborhoods were still segregated, so separate African American communities formed in each city.
Musicians trained in country blues began playing together in groups instead of alone, and a new style developed: urban blues.

Urban blues groups had a rhythm section of bass, drums, guitar, or piano, plus solo instruments like the saxophone, and the band accompanied the singer, answered the singer's lines, and played instrumental choruses.
The piano was loud enough to solo, but an unamplified guitar didn't project well, so it mostly strummed rhythm until the invention of the electric guitar.
Aaron Thibeaux Walker, known as T-Bone Walker, 1910 to 1975, was one of the first musicians to use the electric guitar as a solo blues instrument.
He grew up in Texas playing country blues in the style of Blind Lemon Jefferson, but later developed a flashy solo style of highly embellished melodies.
He was also a showman who played the guitar behind his back, and he strongly influenced the blues guitarist B.B.
King and the rock guitarist Chuck Berry.
First, T-Bone Walker.

Now Blind Lemon Jefferson, Walker's Texas model, who played with the same loose rhythm as delta singers like Robert Johnson, but with much longer and more complex guitar fills between his vocal phrases.
Three O'Clock Blues, by B.B. King, 1951.
Urban blues.
King was a Mississippi born guitarist whose expressive solo style influenced Eric Clapton, Jimi Hendrix, and many other rock guitarists.
Listen for his guitar fills answering and imitating his singing, bending strings to reach blue notes, over soft, sustained saxophone chords.
items.lyr: It's three o'clock in the morning and he can't sleep, because the woman he loves has left him. He's so low that he talks about ending it all, and says goodbye to everyone. "Three o'clock in the morning" is a classic blues image of the loneliest, sleepless hour.
nl: B.B.
King, 1925 to 2015, came from Mississippi, the home of the delta blues.
B.B. came from his nickname, Blues Boy, and his real name was Riley B.
King.
The listening guide is Three O'Clock Blues, from 1951, number one on the Billboard rhythm and blues charts for five weeks.

It's a slow twelve bar blues, at about 76 beats per minute, in which King sings and then answers each vocal line with his guitar, imitating and expanding the melody, and using string bends to reach blue notes.
Saxophones accompany with long held chords, and the drums are very soft, with little accent on the backbeat.
A touch of urban sophistication is the half step slide into some of the chords.
In the lyrics, he wakes in the early morning to find his lover gone, and the local pool hall may be his only comfort.
Compared to the rhythmic freedom of Robert Johnson, the regular beat and structure here show the urbanization of the blues, and King's guitar lines are as important as the lines he sings.
King once said that when he plays, he can hear himself singing.
His lyrical, expressive style influenced many rock guitarists, including Eric Clapton, Jimmy Page, Jimi Hendrix, and Mike Bloomfield.

n: First, Eric Clapton, who said he didn't think there was a better blues guitarist in the world than B.B.
King, playing here with King himself.
Jimmy Page, with Led Zeppelin.
Jimi Hendrix.
Mike Bloomfield.
King performed with jazz bands, groups of every size, and orchestras, and in 1988 he appeared with U2 in their movie Rattle and Hum.
Before going on stage, he asked U2's guitarist, the Edge, to take care of the chords, showing his preference for playing melodic lines.
On his 1993 album Blues Summit, King played duets with John Lee Hooker, Lowell Fulson, and Robert Cray.
We'll hear Hooker later in this chapter.
First, Lowell Fulson.
Robert Cray.
The book's point about urban blues is that it was more complex than country blues, but not necessarily better, and rock musicians drew from both.
Chicago was one of the cities that drew many African American workers during World War One, and its African American population more than doubled again during World War Two.
Chicago musicians formed groups and switched to electric guitars, and their style, called Chicago blues, combined swing jazz and boogie woogie piano with the passion of the delta blues.
Much of the credit goes to Chess Recording Studios, run by the brothers Phil and Leonard Chess, who had immigrated from Poland.
Almost all the blues artists in this chapter recorded for Chess, which gave rural players backup bands and amplification that made their sound urban.
Not every blues sounding song follows the twelve bar form: some stay on a single chord the whole time and keep the blues feel through blue notes and uneven beat subdivisions.
Willie Dixon, 1915 to 1992, worked at Chess as a songwriter, producer, contractor, bass player, and occasional singer, but he is best known as a songwriter.
His songs include You Shook Me, I Can't Quit You Baby, Little Red Rooster, and Hoochie Coochie Man.
Little Red Rooster and I Can't Quit You Baby follow the twelve bar form, while You Shook Me and Hoochie Coochie Man stretch the first A section to eight bars, making each chorus sixteen bars long.
Muddy Waters, from Rolling Fork, Mississippi, used his real name, McKinley Morganfield, as a songwriter, and legend says his nickname came from catching fish by hand in muddy water.
His early hits, like Rollin' Stone from 1948, were close to country blues, with the whining sound of a bottleneck guitar.
Rollin' Stone isn't a twelve bar blues: it stays on one chord throughout, with lyrics in eight bar sections, and gets its blues feel from bent blue notes and a relaxed, uneven beat.
When Muddy Waters switched to electric guitar and added a band, his sound changed from country blues to the urban blues he's best known for.
The band included Little Walter on blues harp, which is the harmonica, Jimmy Rogers on guitar, and Muddy's half brother, Otis Spann, on piano.
First, Little Walter.
Jimmy Rogers.
Otis Spann.
Muddy Waters never actually played rock and roll, but he often performed at rock concerts, including the Band's farewell concert in 1976, which became the movie The Last Waltz.
Hoochie Coochie Man, by Muddy Waters, 1954, written by Willie Dixon.
Chicago blues.
Waters was a Mississippi slide guitarist who went electric in Chicago and recorded for Chess Records.
Listen for the stop time riff, where the band plays a short pattern and then stops so his voice is alone, and for the extra long sixteen bar choruses.
items.lyr: A boast about having supernatural powers with women. A "hoochie coochie man" is a man full of sexual power (the hoochie coochie was an erotic dance). A gypsy fortune teller predicted his birth, and he carries good-luck charms from African American folk magic, called hoodoo: a "black cat bone," a "mojo" (a charm bag), and "John the Conqueroo" (a root carried for luck). He was born on the seventh hour of the seventh day of the seventh month, and seven is a magic number.
nl: He also toured with Eric Clapton in 1979, won many Grammy awards, and died in 1983 after more than forty years of performing the blues.
The listening guide is Willie Dixon's song, I'm Your Hoochie Coochie Man, recorded by Muddy Waters in 1954, which reached number three on the rhythm and blues charts but never made the pop charts.
Its vocal choruses have four extra bars in the first A section, making them sixteen bars, and each A section includes a two beat stop time, where the band briefly stops.
The drums keep an uneven beat with little backbeat, while the piano sometimes slips into even subdivisions, creating a polyrhythm against the drums.
The lyrics boast of supernatural sexual power, with a gypsy fortune teller, a mojo, and a birth on the seventh hour of the seventh day of the seventh month.
As Willie Dixon put it, most blues singers were singing sad blues, but Muddy gave his blues a little pep.

n: Elmore James, 1918 to 1963, claimed he had played with Robert Johnson, who suggested he slide a metal pipe along the strings the way others used a bottleneck.

Like Muddy Waters, he moved from Mississippi to Chicago, where he was among the first delta musicians to work regularly with saxophone, piano, and drums, earning a reputation as an early modernizer of the delta blues.
His groups sounded modern, but his own playing remained bottleneck country blues, a mix you can hear in his recording of Robert Johnson's twelve bar blues, I Believe I'll Dust My Broom.
When he died of a heart attack in 1963, six women claimed to have been married to him.

His slide style was copied by many rock guitarists, including the British players Eric Clapton, Brian Jones of the Rolling Stones, and Jeremy Spencer of the original Fleetwood Mac, and the Americans Jimi Hendrix and Duane Allman.
First, Elmore James.
Brian Jones, playing slide with the Rolling Stones.
Jeremy Spencer, with Fleetwood Mac, on an Elmore James song.
Duane Allman, with the Allman Brothers Band.
Chester Arthur Burnett first called himself Big Foot Chester, but the wolf like growls and howls in his act earned him the name Howlin' Wolf, 1910 to 1976.
He played guitar and harp, and claimed to have played with Robert Johnson, who influenced his guitar style, and with the original Sonny Boy Williamson, who taught him harp.
His aggressive, sometimes raunchy sound didn't suit the pop charts.
Some of his songs are twelve bar blues, but others aren't: Smokestack Lightnin' is chanted over a single chord.
Now the original Sonny Boy Williamson, Howlin' Wolf's harmonica teacher.
Howlin' Wolf recorded Willie Dixon's Little Red Rooster, a traditional twelve bar blues later played by blues revivalists such as the Rolling Stones and the Grateful Dead.
First, the Rolling Stones.
The Grateful Dead.
Howlin' Wolf's songs were also recorded by the British groups Cream, the Yardbirds, and Led Zeppelin, and by the American bands the Doors and the Electric Flag.
First, Cream.
The Yardbirds.
Led Zeppelin.
The Doors.
The Electric Flag.

In 1972, Howlin' Wolf recorded The London Sessions with rock musicians who had begun their careers playing his music: Eric Clapton, Steve Winwood, and Bill Wyman and Charlie Watts of the Rolling Stones.
He died of kidney disease in 1976.
John Lee Hooker, 1917 to 2001, was based in Detroit rather than Chicago, but toured with the Chicago bluesmen.
His dramatic, delta based guitar and deep, rich voice gave him a career of almost six decades.
His twelve bar blues Boom Boom became a rock hit for the British group the Animals in 1965.

Both recordings use a break, where the instruments stop during the vocal line and then answer on the following beats, an effective kind of call and response used in other blues and blues rock recordings.
First, Hooker's original.
The Animals' version.
Other Hooker songs were recorded by the Spencer Davis Group, and by the later American blues revivalists Canned Heat and George Thorogood.
First, the Spencer Davis Group.
Canned Heat.
George Thorogood, with a Hooker song.

n: Hooker appeared in the 1980 film The Blues Brothers and kept recording and touring into the nineties, stopping in 1995.
His 1988 album The Healer featured Santana, Bonnie Raitt, Robert Cray, Canned Heat, Los Lobos, George Thorogood, and Charlie Musselwhite.
First, the title track, with Santana.
Bonnie Raitt, with Hooker.

items.h: Chess Records and the Billboard charts
n: After Leonard Chess died in 1969, the Chess company was sold and stopped promoting careers, but its recordings were preserved and are still being reissued.
The blues is one of the most important roots of rock, but the blues by itself is not rock.
A side note on chart listings: Billboard magazine began in 1894, but only started its charts in 1940.

Because neighborhoods and radio stations were segregated, Billboard had three charts: popular, now called pop; hillbilly, later country and western and now country; and sepia, later called race and now rhythm and blues.

So the rhythm and blues charts reflected African American tastes, the country charts reflected white tastes, especially in the South and West, and the pop charts reflected the largest, mostly white audience.
Rhythm and blues was called race music until the end of the forties.
It was rhythmic dance music that accented the second and fourth beats of each bar, the backbeat, while most other music accented the first and third.
The blues reflected the problems of African American life, but rhythm and blues was dance music that expressed the enjoyment of life.

It came from African American city neighborhoods and was played by rehearsed groups with wild stage shows, where saxophone players swiveled their hips and rolled on the floor while playing, and singers shouted their lyrics.
That energy and backbeat became the basis of fifties rock and roll, while the sexually suggestive lyrics contributed to the backlash against rock.
Louis Jordan, 1908 to 1975, played alto saxophone and clarinet in large jazz bands before forming his own group, Louis Jordan and His Tympany Five.
They played big theaters like the Apollo in New York and the Regal in Chicago, where he was loved for his humor as much as his music.
He called his style shuffle boogie or jumpin' jive, and his group was known as a jump band, as popular with white audiences as with African Americans.

Jordan influenced white rock musicians such as Bill Haley, who imitated his shuffle beat in the early fifties, and later tributes include Joe Jackson's 1981 album Jumpin' Jive and the 1990 musical Five Guys Named Moe.
He was also a big influence on the jump blues style of Little Richard.
First, Bill Haley.
Joe Jackson.
Little Richard.
Bo Diddley, by Bo Diddley, 1955.
Rhythm and blues, and early rock.
Bo Diddley was a Chicago guitarist who called himself a rhythm fanatic and played the guitar like a drum.
Listen for the Bo Diddley beat, repeated on guitar, drums, and maracas the whole time over a single chord, with no chord changes at all.
items.lyr: Built on the old lullaby "Hush, Little Baby," where a parent promises a child gifts. Here the mythical Bo Diddley tries everything to win his "pretty baby": he buys her a diamond ring, and when that fails he turns to black magic ("mojo"). Despite all his effort, she won't have him.
nl: Bo Diddley, born Ellas Bates, 1928 to 2008, strummed his guitar in a constant, throbbing rhythm that sounded almost like drums.

He studied violin before switching to guitar, which went over better in his rough Chicago neighborhood, and he said his friends named him Bo Diddley when he was a boxer, though the name may also come from the diddley bow, a one string instrument of African origin.

His music was considered rhythm and blues in the fifties, and his only top forty pop hit was Say Man, which reached number twenty in 1959, but his first record, Bo Diddley backed with I'm a Man, was number one on the rhythm and blues charts.
The listening guide is the song Bo Diddley, from 1955, at about 104 beats per minute.
It isn't in blues form: it stays on a single chord, in irregular phrases of seventeen, twenty four, and nineteen bars.

The maracas keep even subdivisions, and the rhythm known as the Bo Diddley beat repeats throughout, while between vocal sections he slides a bottleneck between the fifth and seventh frets to suggest chord changes.
He didn't invent the beat, but it carries his name because he popularized it and played it with such energy.
In the lyrics, the mythical Bo Diddley tries everything, from a diamond ring to black magic, but his pretty baby still won't go for it.
He called himself a rhythm fanatic who played the guitar as if he were playing drums.

n: British blues revival groups covered his songs: the Yardbirds did I'm a Man, the Rolling Stones did Mona, and the Animals did Bo Diddley.
In I'm a Man, the harp and piano stop during the vocals, while the drums keep repeating the Bo Diddley beat.
First, the Yardbirds.
The Rolling Stones, with Mona, which, like the song Bo Diddley, stays on one chord.

items.h: Songs with the Bo Diddley beat
n: The Bo Diddley beat has been used in many rock songs, including Buddy Holly's Not Fade Away, Johnny Otis's Willie and the Hand Jive, the Who's Magic Bus, Bruce Springsteen's She's the One, U2's Desire, and the Pretenders' Cuban Slide.
Listen for the beat in each.
First, Buddy Holly.

n: The Pretenders.
The Animals also recorded a tribute, The Story of Bo Diddley, which gave him much of the credit for starting rock and roll.
He kept performing into the nineties, and his influence shows in younger blues musicians like George Thorogood.
One of the most important rhythm and blues pianists was Professor Longhair, Henry Roeland Byrd, 1918 to 1980, from New Orleans.
His rollicking boogie woogie bass lines were based on a piano style developed by African Americans in the South in the twenties, which became basic to most rock piano.

In boogie woogie, the left hand plays a fast repeated pattern of two notes per beat, doubling the basic beat for a driving effect, while the right hand plays short repeated bits of melody called riffs.
Boogie woogie usually follows the twelve bar blues, but Longhair also used pop song forms, as in his 1949 hit Bald Head.
His Mardi Gras in New Orleans is still played every year as the carnival's theme song.
He influenced the rock styles of Fats Domino, Huey Piano Smith, Dr.
John, and Allen Toussaint.

To recap chapter two.
In urban blues, the guitar moved from accompaniment to solo instrument, playing alongside piano, drums, and horns.
Chicago blues was urban blues heavily influenced by swing jazz and boogie woogie piano, and urban blues led directly to fifties rock guitar.
Rhythm and blues used blue notes but usually not the twelve bar form, and it was meant as lighthearted dance music rather than a reflection of hardship.
It was played from rehearsed arrangements, yet performed wildly and full of sexual innuendo, and both its sexuality and its backbeat became basic characteristics of rock.
End of chapter two.

chapters.title: Chapter 3
chapters.sub: Gospel and Country Roots of Rock

items.s: How Far Am I from Canaan?
n: How Far Am I from Canaan, by the Soul Stirrers, with Sam Cooke singing lead, 1952.
Black gospel.
The Soul Stirrers were an influential Texas gospel group, and Cooke later became a soul and pop star.
Listen for Cooke's melismas, sliding around notes before landing on them, and for the moment the tempo doubles halfway through.
items.lyr: Canaan is the Promised Land in the Bible, used here to mean heaven. The singer longs to get there, to hear the angels singing, to see his mother again, and to meet his Savior. The repeated question, "how far am I," admits he still has struggles ahead before he arrives.

n: Oh Happy Day, by the Edwin Hawkins Singers, 1969.
Gospel, in a large choir style with a rock beat.
Edwin Hawkins was an Oakland pianist and arranger whose choir took gospel onto the pop charts.
Listen for soloist Dorothy Morrison's melismas against the choir's plainer answers, and the clapping on the backbeat.
items.lyr: Joy about the day the singer was converted to Christianity: Jesus "washed my sins away," an image of baptism. He also taught the singer to watch, fight, and pray, and to live rejoicing every day. In other words: being saved is a happy day, but life still takes effort.

n: Crying in the Chapel, by the Orioles, 1953.
Doo-wop.
The Orioles were a Baltimore vocal group, and this cover of a country song was one of the first African American hits on the pop charts.
Listen for Sonny Til's gospel style turns in the lead, over the group's soft ahs and a shuffle beat with a strong backbeat.
items.lyr: Someone saw the singer crying in a small, plain chapel (a little church) and thought he was sad, but they were tears of joy. He searched everywhere for happiness and only found peace of mind by praying humbly. He tells the listener to take their troubles to the chapel too.

n: Sh-Boom, by the Chords, 1954.
Doo-wop.
The Chords were an African American vocal group from New York, and this is the original version of the song.
Listen for the solo bass singer on the bridge and the jazzy tenor saxophone solo, so you can compare them with the white cover that comes next.
items.lyr: A dreamy love song: life could be a dream, a paradise, if the singer could be with the one he loves and she would love him back. "Sh-boom" and the other sounds are nonsense syllables that imitate a heartbeat or simply sound happy. There is no deeper story.

n: Sh-Boom, by the Crew-Cuts, 1954.
A pop cover of the Chords' doo-wop hit.
The Crew-Cuts were a white group from Canada, and their version outsold the original, hitting number one for seven weeks.
Listen for the full swing band, the kettledrum, and the dramatic pauses, and notice that the bass solo and the sax solo are gone.
items.lyr: Same lyrics as the Chords' version: life could be a dream if he could be with his love. Only the nonsense syllables change, to more "sh-boom" and "la la la."

n: There Goes My Baby, by the Drifters, 1959.
Rhythm and blues vocal group, with Ben E. King singing lead.
This was the first rhythm and blues record with a full orchestral string section, produced by Leiber and Stoller.
Listen for the swirling violins and booming kettledrums behind the voices, with no backbeat.
items.lyr: He watches the woman he loves walk away. She left without saying why, and he wonders whether she loves him and whether she'll come back. He regrets that he never told her how much he loved her.

items.s: I'll Never Get Out of This World Alive
n: I'll Never Get Out of This World Alive, by Hank Williams, 1952.
Honky-tonk country.
Williams was one of country's greatest songwriters, and this was his last single before he died at twenty nine.
Listen for the steel guitar and fiddles sliding between notes, the two beat bass, and his nasal voice with its little crying hiccups.
items.lyr: A comic list of bad luck: his fishing pole breaks, his rich uncle's will leaves him nothing, his shoes are worn out, and everything goes wrong. "I'll never get out of this world alive" is a joke: nobody does. He decides not to worry, since nothing will work out anyway. It became sadly ironic when he died months later.

n: I Walk the Line, by Johnny Cash, 1956.
Country, from Sun Records, the same label as Elvis.
Cash, known as the Man in Black, crossed over from the country charts to the pop charts with this song.
Listen for the muffled boom chicka guitar, made by weaving wax paper through the strings, and the two beat bass.
items.lyr: A promise of faithfulness. "Walking the line" means staying on the right path and behaving yourself, and here it means staying true to the woman he loves. He keeps a close watch on his heart and keeps his eyes wide open, meaning he won't be tempted by anyone else while they're apart.

n: I'm Walkin', by Fats Domino, 1956.
New Orleans rhythm and blues and rock and roll.
Domino was a pianist and singer from New Orleans whose friendly voice was popular with both white and African American audiences.
Listen for the hand claps on the backbeat, the shuffle rhythm, and the growling tenor saxophone solo.
items.lyr: He's walking and talking, hoping his baby will come back to him. He's lonely, and he's going to keep walking until she returns. "Walking" stands for his effort to win her back.

items.s: School Day (Ring! Ring! Goes the Bell)
n: School Day, by Chuck Berry, 1957.
Rock and roll.
Berry was a guitarist, singer, and songwriter from Saint Louis, often called the Father of Rock Guitar.
Listen for the breaks at the end of each chorus, where the band stops and he sings alone, and for his guitar answering each vocal line.
items.lyr: A teenager's school day from start to finish: getting up early, a hard teacher, a crowded lunch, and the clock dragging. At three o'clock the bell rings and he runs to the local "juke joint" (a hangout with a jukebox), drops a coin in the slot, and dances. The closing lines hail rock and roll as a release from the old, boring ways of the adult world.

n: Long Tall Sally, by Little Richard, 1956.
Rock and roll, with roots in jump blues and gospel.
Little Richard was a pianist and singer from Macon, Georgia, famous for his wild energy, shrieks, and flamboyant image.
Listen for the stop time, where the band hits single chords and drops out so his voice is alone, and the pounding piano.
items.lyr: Gossip played for laughs. He's going to tell Aunt Mary that Uncle John was out with "Long Tall Sally," a tall, flashy woman. When Uncle John sees Aunt Mary coming, he ducks back into the alley to hide. The singer wants to have some fun with Sally himself tonight. "Built for speed" means she's fast and exciting.

n: Shake, Rattle and Roll, by Joe Turner, 1954.
Jump blues, or rhythm and blues.
Turner was a blues shouter from Kansas City who sang over honking saxophones.
Listen for the boogie woogie piano, the hand claps on the backbeat, and the jazzy baritone sax solo, so you can compare it with Bill Haley's cover next.
items.lyr: A man complains to his woman: she stays in bed instead of cooking, wears revealing dresses, and spends his money. Much of it is sexual double meaning: "shake, rattle and roll" means both dancing and sex, and "a one-eyed cat peeping in a seafood store" is a deliberately rude joke. That's why Bill Haley's cover changed many lines.

n: Shake, Rattle and Roll, by Bill Haley and His Comets, 1954.
Rock and roll, from a former western swing bandleader.
Haley's version is faster and cleaned up for white radio audiences.
Listen for the slapped country bass, and the saxophone and guitar playing the riff together instead of a jazz solo.
items.lyr: The same basic complaint, but the sexual lines are removed: instead of being in bed, she's told to get out of the kitchen, and instead of revealing dresses she's cold and treats him wrong. The "one-eyed cat" line stayed, probably because most listeners wouldn't catch the joke.

n: Hound Dog, by Willie Mae Big Mama Thornton, 1952, written by Leiber and Stoller.
Rhythm and blues.
Thornton was a powerful blues singer, and her version was number one on the rhythm and blues charts for seven weeks.
Listen for her rough, commanding voice, the bluesy guitar bending notes, and the very strong backbeat from claps and drums.
items.lyr: A woman throws out a man who has been cheating on her and living off her. In African American slang, a "hound dog" is a man who chases other women. "Wag your tail" mocks him like a begging dog; she's done feeding him.

n: Hound Dog, by Elvis Presley, 1956.
Rock and roll.
Elvis's version was number one on the pop charts for eleven weeks, and it changes the meaning of Thornton's song.
Listen for the faster tempo, the drum hits on the backbeat, the country style guitar solo, and the backup singers holding long chords.
items.lyr: The lyrics were changed: now it's a man insulting someone as worthless, like a hound dog that "ain't never caught a rabbit," a useless hunting dog. "You ain't no friend of mine" and claims of being "high-classed" become lies he sees through. The cheating-man meaning of the original is gone.

n: Burning Love, by Elvis Presley, 1972.
Rock.
This was Elvis's last top ten hit, from his later career.
Listen for the strong backbeat, the mix of straight and swung rhythms, and the backup singers breaking into black gospel style at the end.
items.lyr: He's so full of love and desire that he feels like he's on fire: burning, his temperature rising, flames licking at his body. "A hunk, a hunk of burning love" means a big piece of passion. It's playful exaggeration, not a story.

n: Blue Suede Shoes, by Carl Perkins, 1956.
Rockabilly.
Perkins was a Tennessee singer, guitarist, and songwriter at Sun Records, and this song was number one on the country charts and number two on pop and rhythm and blues.
Listen for the stop time openings, where his voice is alone except for hits on the beat, the slapped bass, and the drummer playing on the rim.
items.lyr: You can do anything to me: knock me down, burn my house, steal my car, drink my liquor. Just don't step on my new blue suede shoes. The shoes stand for a young man's pride and style. The opening ("one for the money...") is a traditional children's countdown before a race, and "cat" is slang for a cool guy.

n: Summertime Blues, by Eddie Cochran, 1958.
Rockabilly.
Cochran was a young rockabilly star who played and sang every part on this record himself, through overdubbing.
Listen for the instrumental breaks between his lines, and the deep voice he uses to play the boss, his parents, and a congressman.
items.lyr: A teenager complains about his summer: he has to work, and when he asks his boss for time off, the boss says no. His parents won't let him use the car because he didn't work late. He even writes to his congressman, who says he's too young to vote. "Raise a fuss, raise a holler" means complain loudly, and "there ain't no cure for the summertime blues" means nobody will help him.

n: Peggy Sue, by Buddy Holly, 1957.
Rock and roll.
Holly was a singer, guitarist, and songwriter from Lubbock, Texas, and one of the first rock guitarists to play a solid body electric guitar.
Listen for the nonstop tom tom drumming, the hiccups in his voice, and the guitar solo suddenly bursting out louder.
items.lyr: A simple love song: if you knew Peggy Sue, you'd understand why he loves her so much. He repeats her name and says she's pretty, and that he longs for her. The word play and repetition matter more than any story.

n: Before chapter five, the book introduces the decade of the sixties.
The decade began with optimism under the young new president, John F.
Kennedy, who promised to beat the Soviet Union in both the missile gap and the space race, and set the goal of putting a man on the moon by the end of the decade, a goal reached in 1969.

His fight against communism had setbacks: the failed Bay of Pigs invasion of Cuba in 1961, and the Cuban missile crisis, which he resolved, but only after bringing the world closer than ever to nuclear war.
He was assassinated in 1963, after only about a thousand days in office.
The civil rights movement grew underneath that optimism.

In 1960, four African American college students sat down at a whites only Woolworth lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, and were refused service, and within two weeks these peaceful sit-ins had spread across the country.
Violence followed too, with riots in fifty eight cities between 1964 and 1967, the worst in Watts in Los Angeles, Newark, and Detroit.
Doctor Martin Luther King worked to keep protests peaceful, while Malcolm X warned of a powder keg about to explode, and both men were assassinated, Malcolm X in 1965 and King in 1968.

There were also legal victories: the Twenty-Fourth Amendment of 1964 outlawed poll taxes, the Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned discrimination in most public places, King's 1965 march from Selma to Montgomery led to the Voting Rights Act, Thurgood Marshall became the first African American Supreme Court justice in 1967, and the 1968 Housing Act outlawed discrimination in housing.
The Vietnam War was the most controversial issue of all.

Presidents Truman, Eisenhower, and Kennedy sent advisers and then troops to keep South Vietnam from communist takeover, and President Johnson escalated with more troops and bombing, at first with wide public support.

By 1966, veterans' reports of destroyed villages, wasted aid, and soldiers returning with drug problems, along with rising casualties, turned many Americans against the war, leading to protests on college campuses and young men avoiding the draft, while others still saw it as a necessary fight against communism.
The war continued until Saigon fell in 1975, and returning veterans received little support.

Other movements began as well: Rachel Carson's 1962 book Silent Spring warned about pesticides like DDT, and Betty Friedan's 1963 book The Feminine Mystique launched the women's liberation movement, attacking the idea that women belonged only at home and the practice of paying men more for the same work.
The hippie movement rejected mainstream society, with psychedelic drugs, beads, and headbands as its symbols.

Much of its optimism ended with the drug related deaths of Jimi Hendrix and Janis Joplin in 1970 and Jim Morrison of the Doors in 1971, and with a killing at the Rolling Stones' Altamont festival in 1969.
First, Jimi Hendrix.
Janis Joplin.
Jim Morrison, with the Doors.
The Rolling Stones, whose 1969 Altamont festival ended in violence.
Chapter five: Teen-Styled Rock Music.
By 1960, most of the strongest performers of mid fifties rock had stopped performing, leaving no competition for the lighter pop rock that emerged between 1957 and 1960.

Carl Perkins stayed out of music after his 1956 car accident, Little Richard entered the ministry, Jerry Lee Lewis's records were banned over his marriage to his young cousin, Elvis Presley was in the army, and Chuck Berry was on trial under the Mann Act and later went to prison.
Buddy Holly, the Big Bopper, and Ritchie Valens died in the 1959 plane crash, and Eddie Cochran was killed in the 1960 car accident that badly injured Gene Vincent.

Some of these performers had already sensed that pop was the future: Presley was recording more pop than rockabilly at RCA, and Holly's It Doesn't Matter Anymore and Cochran's Three Steps to Heaven were pop songs.
Rockabilly artists who refused to change, like Gene Vincent and Ronnie Hawkins, left to perform in England and Canada, where rockabilly was still popular.
Here's Ronnie Hawkins.

Payola means paying for airplay or other publicity, and some form of it existed as far back as the Civil War, when vaudeville performers agreed to sing a song at every show in return for having their photo printed on its sheet music.
By the late fifties, payola meant paying radio and television programmers to play particular songs, so that money, rather than quality, decided what got played.

It wasn't illegal until after the scandal, but it was considered unethical, and small independent labels depended on it, paying for airplay in one town and using the profits to do the same in the next.
The scandal was set off by songwriters, or rather by their representatives.

The Copyright Act of 1909 gave songwriters three ways to be paid: a share of sheet music sales, mechanical fees for each piano roll or recording sold, and performance fees whenever the song was performed in public.

The American Society of Composers, Authors, and Publishers, known as ASCAP, was formed in 1914 to collect performance fees from concert halls, clubs, restaurants, and other venues, and distribute them to its members.

ASCAP generally excluded blues, rhythm and blues, country, and rock writers, so in 1940 broadcasters who resisted ASCAP's fees and monopoly formed Broadcast Music Incorporated, or BMI, which most rock writers of the fifties and early sixties joined.

As rock's popularity cut into its profits, ASCAP looked for ways to discredit the music BMI handled, and in 1958 it asked a congressional committee, already investigating cheating on TV quiz shows, to look into bribes paid to disc jockeys.
That investigation became the payola scandal, and many small labels that had depended on payola for airplay went out of business.
Disc jockey Alan Freed, 1921 to 1965, had fought racism by giving African American artists as much airplay as he could, but he had also accepted a lot of payola.

By then he had his own ABC television show, Dance Party, and although ABC asked him to deny the charges, evidence like his name appearing as a co-writer of Chuck Berry's 1955 hit Maybellene made his guilt obvious.
He pleaded guilty, lost his show, was also convicted of income tax evasion, and died in 1965 as his drinking worsened.
Another disc jockey investigated in the scandal, Dick Clark, 1929 to 2012, escaped ruin.
He hosted the teen dance show American Bandstand, which brought Philadelphia pop music and dances to teenagers all over the country.

It occasionally featured rockabilly and rhythm and blues artists, but much more often clean cut, white teen idols such as Pat Boone, Paul Anka, Frankie Avalon, Connie Francis, Fabian, Bobby Rydell, Brenda Lee, and Bobby Vee, while the leather jackets and rebellious messages of rockabilly had no place there.
Clark did have financial interests in some of the records he promoted, but he was cleared when his lawyers showed he also promoted records he had no stake in.
He had to sell his music business interests but kept his show, largely because the industry saw American Bandstand as a positive influence on teens, while Freed's music was seen as corrupting.

Television brought rock into homes in other ways too: Ed Sullivan added rock performers to his Sunday night family show to attract teenagers, and by 1965 ABC had the prime time rock show Shindig and NBC had Hullabaloo.
We'll hear most of those teen idols later in the chapter.
First, Bobby Vee, who isn't discussed further.
items.s: Take Good Care of My Baby

n: Tutti Frutti, by Little Richard, 1955. The original, to compare with the cover that follows.
It reached number seventeen on the pop charts and number two on the rhythm and blues charts.
Listen for his growling, no holds barred vocal with octave leap oohs, the jazz style walking bass, and the drummer's strongly accented backbeat.
items.lyr: Twelve bar blues form, with stop time breaks where the voice is alone. He sings about rocking with Sue (rocking was slang for sex) and hints that Daisy knows how to love him too, so he may not be true to Sue.
nl: Most teen idols, especially the men, sang in the style of the crooners of the twenties through the forties, such as Perry Como and Bing Crosby.
Pat Boone, born in 1934, became popular singing pop ballads as well as covers of blues and rhythm and blues songs.
He changed those songs differently than the rockabilly singers had, because he wasn't after rockabilly's energy, and his recordings fit his clean cut, boy next door image.
While Carl Perkins and Elvis dared anyone to step on their blue suede shoes, Boone's trademark was clean white buck shoes.
The book compares Little Richard's original Tutti Frutti, which reached number seventeen pop and number two rhythm and blues, with Boone's cover, which reached number twelve pop.
Little Richard's version, from 1955, is a twelve bar blues at about 172 beats per minute.

It opens with a two bar introduction of nonsense syllables that shows off his no holds barred vocal style, punctuated by leaping oohs, and the last four bars of some choruses are sung over stop time breaks.
The piano plays even subdivisions against the uneven beat, with a jazz style walking bass, saxophone punctuations, and a strong backbeat on the drums.
In the lyrics, rocking with Sue was slang for sex, and Daisy knows how to love him too, hinting that he isn't faithful to Sue.
First, Little Richard's original.

n: Tutti Frutti, by Pat Boone, 1956.
Teen idol pop, a cover of Little Richard.
Boone was a clean cut, boy next door crooner, famous for his white buck shoes, and his version reached number twelve on the pop charts, higher than the original.
Listen for how he imitates Little Richard's rhythmic phrasing without his growl, the smoother and more polite voice, and the weaker backbeat.
items.lyr: Same twelve bar blues form and almost the same tempo. Boone removed the sexual references: no rocking, and instead of having two girlfriends he admits Daisy tempts him but stays true to Sue. He said he changed words that seemed too raw for him.
nl: Pat Boone's version, from 1956, is slightly faster, at about 176 beats per minute.
He imitates Little Richard's rhythmic singing and inflections, but without his growl, and his voice sounds smoother, more controlled, and polite.
A backup group sings ahs, the beat subdivisions are uneven throughout, the backbeat is less obvious, and the only jazz touch left is the tenor saxophone solo.
Boone removed the sexual references: there's no rocking with Sue, and instead of having two girlfriends, he admits Daisy tempts him but stays true to Sue.
Boone said he changed some words because they seemed too raw for him, and Little Richard joked that white kids put Pat Boone's record on the bed and hid his in the drawer.

Many rock fans would say Boone wasn't a rock singer at all, but the book argues his Tutti Frutti counts as rock because of its historical context: it represents the pop direction rock followed for the rest of the fifties and into the sixties.

n: Movies and television supported the clean teen idol image.
Pat Boone played teenagers in the movies April Love, in 1957, and Journey to the Center of the Earth, in 1959.

Once American Bandstand was broadcast nationwide, it introduced the Philadelphia teen idols Frankie Avalon, Fabian, and Bobby Rydell, who were then promoted further by movies such as Beach Blanket Bingo, starring Frankie Avalon and Annette Funicello, a former Mouseketeer from The Mickey Mouse Club.
We'll hear Avalon and Rydell with songs the book names later.
First, Fabian, whose real name was Fabian Forte.
Annette Funicello.
Ricky Nelson, 1940 to 1985, was more important to rock for his rockabilly recordings, but his appearances on his parents' TV show, The Adventures of Ozzie and Harriet, gave him a teen idol image.
Two of the most successful female singers of the teen idol era were Connie Francis, born Concetta Franconero, and Brenda Lee, born Brenda Mae Tarpley.
We'll hear Connie Francis with a song the book names later.
First, Brenda Lee.
Most teen idols succeeded more through their looks and how much teenagers identified with them than through musical talent.
Their natural but untrained voices captured youthful enthusiasm, and on TV, in movies, and even in live shows they usually lip synced to their records.
They rarely played instruments beyond some simple guitar chords, and they generally didn't write songs.

Paul Anka, born in 1941, was the exception: he wrote many of his own hits, as well as hits for others, including It Doesn't Matter Anymore for Buddy Holly, My Way for Frank Sinatra, and She's a Lady for Tom Jones, along with the theme music for Johnny Carson's Tonight Show.
First, Frank Sinatra's My Way.
Tom Jones, with another Anka song.
Venus, by Frankie Avalon, 1959.
Teen idol pop.
Avalon was one of the Philadelphia teen idols introduced on American Bandstand, and Venus was number one for five weeks.
Listen for the very full production with orchestra, chorus, and drums, and the gentle, sincere mood of his crooning.
items.lyr: He is so desperate for romance that he prays to Venus, the Roman goddess of love, for a girlfriend, but he is also choosy and lists exactly what she should be like. A typical teen idol theme: puppy love and dreaming of the perfect mate.
nl: Teen idol songs were as youthful and wholesome as the singers' images, mostly about the ups and downs of puppy love and dreams of the perfect mate.

Examples include Frankie Avalon's Venus, from 1959, Connie Francis's Where the Boys Are, from 1961, Paul Anka's Puppy Love, from 1960, and, on other teenage concerns, Bobby Rydell's Swingin' School, from 1960.
The listening guide is Venus, number one on the pop charts for five weeks.
It's at about 114 beats per minute, in A A B A form with an eight bar introduction of oohs from a chorus, and a full production with orchestra, chorus, and drums.
The mood is gentle and the singer very sincere.
In the lyrics, he's so desperate for romance that he prays to Venus, the Roman goddess of love, for a girlfriend, though he's also quite picky and lists exactly what he wants.

n: Connie Francis.
Paul Anka.
Bobby Rydell.
Because it featured teenage dancers, American Bandstand started or spread many dance crazes of the late fifties and early sixties.
In the fifties, teens danced the bop to songs like Gene Vincent's Be-Bop-A-Lula and Dance to the Bop, and Danny and the Juniors' At the Hop.
Variations on the bop took animal names, like the Pony, the Chicken, and the Monkey, while the Dog and the Alligator were considered too suggestive for American Bandstand.
First, Gene Vincent's Dance to the Bop.
Danny and the Juniors.
In 1960, a young Philadelphia performer named Ernest Evans covered a song called The Twist, by the blues singer Hank Ballard.
For his stage name, he chose Chubby Checker, a not so subtle variation on Fats Domino's name.
First, Hank Ballard's original.
Chubby Checker's version did more than become a hit: it started a dance craze that lasted several years, with more Twist songs by Checker and others, including the Isley Brothers and Sam Cooke.
Checker's songs also popularized other dances, such as the Pony, the Fly, and the Limbo.
The Isley Brothers.
Sam Cooke.
Latin music is part of the history of American popular music, though Latin rhythms influenced jazz much more than rock.
One Latin rock hit was by the teen idol Ritchie Valens, 1941 to 1959: La Bamba, from 1959, based on a traditional Mexican dance song.
Since pop singers rarely wrote songs, the pop boom created a need for specialized songwriters.
Many pop hits between 1959 and 1963 were written and published in the Brill Building, at 1619 Broadway in New York, or across the street at Al Nevins and Don Kirshner's Aldon Music Company.
Their songs combined influences from gospel, doo-wop, and teen idol music.

Most of the writers worked in teams, the most famous being Howard Greenfield and Neil Sedaka, Barry Mann and Cynthia Weil, Doc Pomus and Mort Shuman, Gerry Goffin and Carole King, Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller, and Jeff Barry and Ellie Greenwich.
Sedaka, Mann, and King were also performers who sang some of their own hits.
First, Neil Sedaka.
items.s: Breaking Up Is Hard to Do

n: Barry Mann.
A song by Doc Pomus and Mort Shuman, recorded by the Drifters.

n: The writer and producer George Shadow Morton worked with Jeff Barry and Ellie Greenwich to create short storyline songs, unusual for pop, such as Remember, Walkin' in the Sand, and Leader of the Pack, both sung by the Shangri-Las in 1964.
First, Remember.
Leader of the Pack.
Female vocal groups such as the Andrews Sisters had been popular from the mid twenties on, singing mainly swing jazz and later adding other styles, including gospel.
Will You Love Me Tomorrow, by the Shirelles, 1960.
Brill Building pop, by a girl group.
It was written by Gerry Goffin and Carole King, and the Shirelles, unusual for the time, also wrote some of their own songs and had twelve top ten hits in four years.
Listen for Shirley Alston's lead backed doo wop style by the other Shirelles, and the orchestral strings playing the fills and the instrumental section.
items.lyr: AABA song form. The singer plans to sleep with her date and is unsure the relationship will last beyond that night. Carole King said it spoke for young women facing the double standard of the time: will you respect me in the morning?
nl: In early sixties popular music, women were still mostly singers rather than instrumentalists, and trios and quartets of female singers, known as girl groups, became popular with teens.
The Shirelles placed twelve top ten hits on the pop charts between 1960 and 1963, and, unusually for pop singers of the time, did some of their own songwriting.
The listening guide is their first number one hit, Will You Love Me Tomorrow, from 1960, written by Carole King and her then husband, Gerry Goffin, a good example of the Brill Building pop sound.
It was number one pop for two weeks and number two rhythm and blues.
At about 138 beats per minute, in A A B A form with even subdivisions, Shirley Alston's lead is backed by the other Shirelles in doo-wop style.
The drums stress the backbeat with two quick notes on beat two and a single accent on beat four, and orchestral strings play fills at phrase endings and the lead in the instrumental section.
The singer plans to sleep with her date and isn't sure the relationship will last beyond that night.

Carole King said the song spoke for young women wondering whether they should or not, and whether he'd still respect them in the morning, cutting to the heart of the sexual double standard of the time.

n: Phil Spector, 1940 to 2021, was a Brill Building writer and producer whose productions were so distinctive that his style became known as the wall of sound.
He used so many instruments, overdubbed and mixed so thoroughly, that they formed a massive wall of instrumental color behind the vocals.
He disliked stereo, because it separated instruments from each other.

When he did let a single instrument stand out, the effect was colorful, as in the Spanish flamenco style guitar fills on the Crystals' Uptown, from 1962, or the natural sound of rain behind the Ronettes' Walking in the Rain, from 1964.
First, the Crystals.
The Ronettes, with Walking in the Rain.
A standard rock drum set wasn't enough for Spector.

He loved classical music, especially the nineteenth century German romantic composer Richard Wagner, and imitated Wagner's colorful use of percussion, adding chimes, castanets, triangles, timpani, and gongs to an already full sound.
His records didn't sound Wagnerian, but they had more orchestral fullness than earlier rock records that used only strings or brass, and he called them symphonies for teens.
Songwriter Ellie Greenwich said his records had a Wagnerian power and intensity, and that everything got bigger and bigger until there was no more record.
Here's Wagner himself.
Spector worked in both New York and Los Angeles, and started his own company, Philles, named for Phil and Lester Sill, who handled the business until Spector took full control late in 1962.
He often owned his groups' names as well as the singers' contracts, so he could use any combination of singers and call them the Crystals, or Bob B.
Soxx and the Blue Jeans.
He presented Darlene Love, whose real name was Darlene Wright, with an unnamed backup group that could change from record to record.
First, Bob B.
Soxx and the Blue Jeans.
