n: Darlene Love.
items.s: (Today I Met) The Boy I'm Gonna Marry

n: Be My Baby, by the Ronettes, 1963.
Girl group, produced by Phil Spector.
Spector's wall of sound overdubbed so many instruments, mixed together in mono, that they blend into one massive background, and he called his records symphonies for teens.
Listen for Ronnie singing the verses alone, the other two answering be my baby in the refrains, and the strings, guitars, keyboards, brass, saxophones, and percussion piled up behind them.
items.lyr: She promises her lover undying love and affection for all eternity, and asks him to be her baby. Spector later married Ronnie, the lead singer.
nl: The one group Spector kept as a regular trio was the Ronettes, and he married their lead singer, Ronnie Bennett, in 1967.
The listening guide is Be My Baby, from 1963, number two pop and number four rhythm and blues.
At about 132 beats per minute, its wall of sound comes from overdubbed strings, guitars, several keyboards, brass, saxophones, and many percussion instruments.
The three Ronettes don't harmonize: Ronnie sings the verses alone, and the other two answer with be my baby in the refrains.
Low strings play the melody in an instrumental section, and a short break punctuated by percussion separates the third and fourth refrains.
In the lyrics, she promises her love and affection forever.

n: Spector kept his reputation for hit records, and was asked to sift through hours of tape by the soon to disband Beatles, add backing, and produce their album Let It Be, recorded in 1969 and released in 1970.
George Harrison and John Lennon both had him produce their solo work, including Harrison's All Things Must Pass and The Concert for Bangladesh, and Lennon's Imagine.
First, the Beatles.
George Harrison, from All Things Must Pass.
John Lennon.
In the mid seventies, Spector tried a comeback producing Cher and Dion, but couldn't recapture his earlier success.
First, Dion.
Cher.

In 1980, he produced the Ramones' album End of the Century, giving the punk band a sound strikingly different from their earlier records, which wall of sound fans liked and most longtime Ramones fans considered a disaster.
His 1991 boxed set was titled Back to Mono, stressing how important mono recording was to his thick sound.
In 2009, Spector was sentenced to nineteen years to life in prison for the shooting death of the actress Lana Clarkson.
items.s: Do You Remember Rock 'n' Roll Radio?

n: While East Coast pop rock was about puppy love and teen dances, West Coast musicians developed their own danceable style, surf rock.

Surf vocals weren't based on the crooner tradition, and surf bands played their own instruments instead of using studio orchestras, in some ways a return to older rock played on guitars, bass, and drums, though the image and sound were light and pop oriented.
Instrumental hits were more common in surf rock than in any earlier style, with saxophones and electric organs, but mostly electric guitar, in the lead.
The surf guitar style was built on three sources: Duane Eddy, the Ventures, and Dick Dale.
Duane Eddy, born in 1938, created a style called twangy guitar by plucking the strings very close to the bridge, where they are tightest, for a strong, nasal attack.
He played repeated lead lines on the guitar's bass strings, with vibrato and studio or amplifier echo, giving a constantly wavering sound that may have reminded surf groups of moving water.
John Fogerty called him the first rock and roll guitar god.
His first hit, Rebel-'Rouser, from 1958, has the energy of gospel music and an instrumental call and response, in which a saxophone answers his guitar.
His next hits were Ramrod, a blues, and Forty Miles of Bad Road, in a standard pop song form.

The Ventures, from Tacoma, Washington, were one of the most important early instrumental groups associated with surf, although they only adopted the surf image after other surf groups had copied them.
They had two guitarists, an electric bassist, and a drummer, with a sound clearly influenced by Duane Eddy's twang.

They were one of the few surf groups to keep their following through the sixties and beyond, recording a version of the theme for the TV show Hawaii Five-O in 1969, and thanks to a large following in Japan, they were still popular when surf music was revived in the United States in the early eighties.
Dick Dale, born Richard Anthony Monsour, 1937 to 2019, was called the King of Surf Guitar, because he created a style copied by many surf groups of the early sixties.

Originally from Boston, he was living in Balboa, California, when his band, Dick Dale and the Del-Tones, began with Duane Eddy's twangy style, as in Let's Go Trippin', from 1961, a blues in form but not in style.
Misirlou, by Dick Dale and the Del Tones, 1961.
Instrumental surf rock.
Dale, the King of Surf Guitar, turned a Greek melody into a showpiece using the tremolo technique of Middle Eastern plucked instruments, which his Lebanese uncle taught him.
Listen for the very fast up and down picking that sustains each note while his other hand slides along the neck, and the amplifier reverb that gives the guitar a wet, surf sound.
items.lyr: No lyrics, only some wordless background vocals. The melody is broken up and varied to show off the guitar. Near the end the rock backbeat drops out for a Middle Eastern rhythm. A slower version was used in the film Pulp Fiction in 1994.
nl: In his version of the Greek melody Misirlou, also from 1961, Dale developed a technique based on the tremolo of Middle Eastern plucked string instruments, meaning very fast repetitions of a note.
As his Lebanese uncle had taught him, he picked a string up and down very fast while sliding his other hand along the fingerboard, creating an impressive effect of speed, and added Eddy's twang.
In the listening guide, at about 192 beats per minute, the form is through composed, meaning the melody is broken up and varied rather than repeated in sections.
It opens with an unmeasured guitar introduction of fast tremolo picking and rapid descending scales, and amplifier reverb gives the guitar a wet sound, like being in the surf.
Once the drums enter they keep a fast beat with a backbeat, breaking five times for guitar solos, and wordless vocals sometimes fill out the melody.
Near the end the backbeat drops out for a Middle Eastern rhythm, and the recording slows down at the very end.

The Beach Boys helped popularize Dale's style by covering his hits, he appeared in the 1987 movie Back to the Beach with Frankie Avalon and Annette Funicello, and Misirlou was used in the soundtrack of Pulp Fiction in 1994.

n: Other instrumental surf groups that followed Eddy, the Ventures, and Dale included the Marketts, the Chantays, and the Surfaris.
Their hits often took titles from surfing: the Chantays' Pipeline, from 1963, is named for the curled shape of a wave, and even skateboarding sidewalk surfers knew what the Surfaris' Wipe Out meant.
Surf performances often had very active drum solos with crashing cymbals, imitating waves crashing on the beach.
First, the Marketts.
The Chantays.
The Surfaris.
Listen for the drum solo.
The Beach Boys were formed in Hawthorne, California, by three brothers, Brian, Carl, and Dennis Wilson, their cousin Mike Love, and a neighbor, Alan Jardine.
The Wilsons' father, Murry Wilson, managed them, and after the success of Surfin', from 1961, he got them a contract with Capitol Records.

They were more than a surf group from the start: guitarist Carl Wilson used Eddy's twang and Dale's tremolo, but also imitated Chuck Berry's riffs, and Brian Wilson, the main writer and producer, based the group's vocal harmonies on the jazz vocal group the Four Freshmen.
Brian Wilson said that when he first heard the Four Freshmen's Day by Day, he loved the sound, and learned all his harmonies from them.
Sweet Little Sixteen, by Chuck Berry, 1958.
Rock and roll.
It reached number two on the pop charts and number one on the rhythm and blues charts, and the Beach Boys later reused its music for the next song.
Listen for Berry's guitar riff running through the song, the boogie woogie piano with long glissandos in the instrumental section, and the breaks where his voice is alone.
items.lyr: A sixteen year old girl tries to talk her parents into letting her go out to rock and roll. The verses name cities across the country where the good rock shows are.
nl: As Brian learned more about studio production, his records came close to the fullness of Phil Spector's wall of sound.

The Beach Boys' 1963 hit Surfin' U.S.A. had the same melody, chords, and form as Chuck Berry's 1958 hit Sweet Little Sixteen, and although Wilson first claimed the writing credit, perhaps believing he'd written it, the credit and royalties eventually went to Berry.
The listening guide compares the two.
Berry's version is at about 176 beats per minute, with uneven subdivisions, a strong backbeat, a guitar riff running through most of the song, and a boogie woogie piano solo with long glissandos.

Its sixteen bar verses are built from an antecedent phrase and a consequent phrase, two phrases on the same chords where the second sounds more final, and the band breaks for a solo voice in some verses.
The lyrics are about a sixteen year old girl begging her parents to let her go out to rock and roll, naming cities with good rock music.
It was number two pop for three weeks and number one rhythm and blues for three weeks.
First, Chuck Berry's original.

n: Surfin U S A, by the Beach Boys, 1963.
Surf rock, with vocals.
It has the same melody, chords, and form as Sweet Little Sixteen. Brian Wilson first claimed the writing credit, but it was eventually given to Chuck Berry.
Listen for the Four Freshmen style vocal harmonies, the imitation of Berry's guitar riff, and the organ and then guitar in the instrumental section.
items.lyr: A song about surfing and surfers. The singer wishes everyone in the country had an ocean and could have fun like the surfers in California, Australia, and Hawaii. Beach names take the place of the cities in Berry's song.
nl: The Beach Boys' version is a little slower, at about 164, with mostly even subdivisions, a strong backbeat, an imitation of Berry's guitar riff rhythm, and an organ and guitar solo.
Its antecedent and consequent phrases match Berry's closely, and the book suggests singing one of Berry's phrases followed by one of theirs to hear that Berry deserved the credit.
The lyrics wish that everyone in the country had an ocean, so they could surf like the surfers in California, Australia, and Hawaii, with surf spots replacing the cities in Berry's song.
It reached number three pop.

n: By late 1963, Brian Wilson had become a fine songwriter, expanding the group beyond beach songs to other teenage interests like school spirit and fast cars.
He also helped write and produce surf and car songs for his friends, the vocal duo Jan and Dean.
By 1966, Brian Wilson had a nervous breakdown and stopped touring, and his place on stage was taken first by Glen Campbell and then by Bruce Johnston.
First, Glen Campbell.
Bruce Johnston, with his early duo Bruce and Terry.
Free from touring, Brian kept writing, producing, singing, and playing on the records, and in 1966 he made the Beach Boys' most important album, Pet Sounds.
It wasn't their biggest seller, but all its songs were connected by a theme, and it sent rock albums in a new direction.
Concept albums existed before, but most rock albums were just collections of unrelated songs.
In Pet Sounds, the concept isn't even hinted at in the title, but emerges song by song: the hopes, dreams, and anxieties of a young person growing up.
Hopes appear in Wouldn't It Be Nice, Don't Talk, and I'm Waiting for the Day, and insecurity in I Know There's an Answer, I Just Wasn't Made for These Times, Caroline, No, and God Only Knows.
Its productions are thick, with many instrumental tracks layered on top of each other, much like Spector's wall of sound.
First, Wouldn't It Be Nice.
God Only Knows.
Caroline, No, the last song, followed by dogs barking and a passing train.
Pet Sounds may have started the concept album trend, but it was the Beatles' Sgt.
Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band, recorded the next year, that inspired other bands to make concept albums.
The Beatles quietly credited Pet Sounds by ending Good Morning Good Morning with animal sounds and a galloping horse, imitating the dogs and train at the end of Caroline, No.
Pet Sounds remains the Beach Boys' most important contribution to rock history because of its enormous influence.
To recap chapter five.
In the late fifties and early sixties, much of what was called rock and roll changed from the energetic blues and country based sound of the mid fifties to a gentler pop sound called teen idol pop.

This happened because established songwriters resented competition from rock musicians who wrote their own songs, because much rock was recorded on small labels hurt by the payola scandal, and because many parents objected to the rebellious, sexy lyrics and dances rooted in African American blues and rhythm and blues.
Teen pop was written for young teens, marketed through movies and radio, and often backed by orchestras instead of guitars, bass, and drums, with the backbeat largely gone.
By the early sixties, the West Coast surf style became popular: surf bands played their own instruments, but their songs were still lighthearted celebrations of youth.
The Beach Boys eventually left surf behind, creating complex studio productions like Spector's wall of sound.
End of chapter five.
